newsitem.title: FRANCE: What's in a name? Euro-court bans "Flower of Mary".
newsitem.headline: What's in a name? Euro-court bans "Flower of Mary".

text.p: A 13-year-old French girl lost a marathon legal battle on Thursday to overturn laws banning her family from naming her "Fleur de Marie" (Flower of Mary).

The European Court of Human Rights, based in Strasbourg, voted by seven to two that a French refusal to register her name on legal documents did not violate the girl's right to respect of private and family life.

French courts have barred the child from being called "Fleur de Marie" -- after the heroine in a novel by 19th century French writer Eugene Sue -- because it does not appear in lists of Roman Catholic saints' names.

French law bars children from having names likely to insult others or that may expose them to teasing. When "Fleur de Marie" Guillot was born in 1983, her birth was registered in the town hall with no entry in the forename column.

In 1984, a court in Nanterre west of Paris ruled that "a forename cannot...consist of a combination of two names linked by a preposition". But it agreed to register the girl's alternative name "Fleur-Marie" submitted by her parents.
"The (European) court was able to understand that Mr and Mrs Guillot had been upset by the refusal to register the forename they had chosen for their daughter," the court said in a statement.

"It noted that that forename consequently could not appear on official documents and deeds," it added. But it said the girl was still known to her family and friends as "Fleur de Marie" without legal hindrance and that French courts had registered her alternative name.
